stem: Which scientist first used the word "cell" after looking at thin slices of cork under a microscope?
explanation: Robert Hooke saw tiny empty boxes in cork in 1665 and called them cells, because they reminded him of small rooms.

stem: The cell theory applies to plants and animals, but not to bacteria.
explanation: False. The cell theory applies to every living thing. A bacterium is a single prokaryotic cell.

stem: Which scientist concluded that all animals are made of cells?
explanation: Schwann studied animal tissues and concluded they are made of cells. Schleiden reached the same conclusion for plants.

stem: What did Rudolf Virchow add to the cell theory?
option_a: All plants are made of cells
option_c: All cells come from pre-existing cells
explanation: Virchow proposed in 1855 that new cells come only from cells that already exist.

stem: Which invention made the discovery of cells possible?
explanation: Cells are too small to see with the naked eye. The microscope let scientists see them for the first time.

stem: According to the cell theory, a living thing can be made of just one cell.
explanation: True. The cell theory says living things are made of one or more cells, and many organisms, like bacteria and amoebas, are a single cell.

stem: Anton van Leeuwenhoek is best known for
option_a: being the first to see living single-celled organisms, in pond water
option_b: naming the cell after looking at cork
option_c: proving that all animals are made of cells
option_d: disproving spontaneous generation with sealed flasks
explanation: Leeuwenhoek built powerful lenses and was the first to see living microorganisms, which he called "animalcules."

stem: A cut on your arm heals as skin cells divide to make new skin cells. Which part of the cell theory does this show?
option_a: All living things are made of cells
option_b: All cells come from pre-existing cells
option_c: The cell is the basic unit of structure
option_d: Cells can form from nonliving material
explanation: The new skin cells come from existing skin cells dividing. They don't appear from nothing.

stem: Which of these is one of the ideas added in the MODERN cell theory?
option_a: All cells are the same size
option_b: Only animals are made of cells
option_d: Cells can form from nonliving material
explanation: The modern cell theory adds that energy flow happens inside cells, that cells pass on DNA when they divide, and that all cells have similar chemistry.

stem: A student says, "A virus is alive because it has DNA." Using the cell theory, why is this claim weak?
option_a: Viruses are too small to see
option_b: Viruses are made of many cells
option_d: Viruses are not made of cells, and the cell theory says living things are made of cells
explanation: Having genetic material isn't enough. Viruses are not cells, so by the cell theory they don't count as living.

stem: Which of these are statements of the cell theory (original or modern)? Choose all that apply.
option_a: All living things are made of one or more cells
option_b: The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
option_c: All cells come from pre-existing cells
option_d: All cells have a cell wall
option_e: Cells contain hereditary information (DNA) that is passed on during division
explanation: The cell theory includes all of these except the cell wall. Animal cells have no cell wall.

stem: A single-celled amoeba eats, grows, responds, and reproduces. Which idea does this support?
option_a: The cell is the basic unit of life, able to carry out all life processes
option_b: Cells can form from nonliving material
explanation: One amoeba cell does everything a living thing must do, which is why the cell is called the basic unit of life.

stem: Why is a heart muscle cell considered alive, while a single protein molecule is not?
option_b: The cell can carry out life processes; a molecule alone cannot
explanation: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out life processes. Molecules are the building materials of cells, but they aren't alive on their own.

stem: The cell theory was developed by one scientist working alone.
explanation: False. Many scientists, including Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow, built on each other's work over about 200 years.

stem: Francesco Redi put meat in open jars and covered jars. Maggots appeared only on meat in the open jars, where flies could land. What did this experiment show?
option_c: Maggots come from flies, not from the meat itself
explanation: Maggots appeared only where flies could lay eggs, so living things come from other living things. This went against spontaneous generation.

stem: Which discovery would go AGAINST the cell theory?
option_a: A new bacterium with no nucleus
option_b: A cell dividing into two cells
option_c: A plant cell with a large vacuole
option_d: A living organism that is not made of cells
explanation: The cell theory says all living things are made of cells. A living thing without cells would break that rule. Bacteria without a nucleus are still cells.

stem: The modern cell theory says all cells have a similar chemical makeup. What does this mean?
option_a: All cells are made mostly of the same kinds of molecules: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids
option_b: All cells are the same shape
option_d: All cells have the same DNA
explanation: From bacteria to brain cells, cells are built from the same four kinds of large molecules.

stem: Cells were first seen in 1665, but the cell theory wasn't complete until the 1850s. What best explains the delay?
option_b: Microscopes had to improve, and scientists needed evidence from many kinds of organisms
explanation: Better microscopes and observations of many plants, animals, and microbes were needed before scientists could say the ideas were true for all living things.

stem: Scientists discover a new single-celled organism near a deep-sea vent. What does the cell theory predict about how new cells of this organism form?
option_a: They form from the hot water
option_c: They form only when existing cells of the organism divide
explanation: All cells come from pre-existing cells, so new cells of this organism come from its existing cells dividing.

stem: Which observations are evidence that all cells come from pre-existing cells? Choose all that apply.
option_a: Watching one cell divide into two under a microscope
option_b: Pasteur's boiled broth staying free of microbes while sealed
option_c: Skin cells dividing to heal a cut
option_d: A rock crumbling into smaller pieces
explanation: Each of the first three shows new cells or microbes coming only from existing cells. A crumbling rock is not alive and says nothing about cells.

stem: A student cuts open a dry bean seed and says, "This is not made of cells because it isn't growing." What is the best response?
option_a: The student is right; only growing things have cells
option_d: The seed is made of cells; the cell theory says all living things are made of cells, even dormant ones
explanation: A dormant seed is alive and made of cells. It will grow when it gets water and warmth.

stem: A student models the cell theory with LEGO: each brick is a cell, and a wall built from bricks is an organism. Which part of the cell theory does this model show best?
option_a: Cells are the basic building blocks (units of structure) of living things
option_b: All cells come from pre-existing cells
explanation: Just as bricks are the units that build a wall, cells are the units that build every organism.

stem: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus. Why don't they go against the cell theory?
option_b: They are still cells, and they came from pre-existing cells; the cell theory doesn't require a nucleus
explanation: Red blood cells form from stem cells in bone marrow and are still cells. The cell theory never says every cell must have a nucleus.

stem: Which observation supports the modern idea that cells pass on hereditary information when they divide?
option_c: Daughter cells have the same DNA as the parent cell
explanation: When a cell divides, each new cell gets a copy of the parent's DNA. That is hereditary information being passed on.

stem: The word "eukaryote" means
explanation: "Eu-" means true and "-karyon" means nucleus. "Pro-" means before, so a prokaryote is "before nucleus."

stem: Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells have a cell membrane.
explanation: True. Every cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA.

stem: Which of these is a prokaryote?
explanation: Bacteria like E. coli are prokaryotes. Mushrooms (fungi), amoebas (protists), and oak trees (plants) are eukaryotes.

stem: How does the size of a typical prokaryotic cell compare with a typical eukaryotic cell?
option_a: Prokaryotic cells are usually much larger
option_b: Prokaryotic cells are usually much smaller
option_c: They are always the same size
explanation: Most prokaryotes are about 1–10 micrometers across, while most eukaryotic cells are about 10–100 micrometers.

stem: In a prokaryotic cell, the region where the DNA is found is called the
explanation: Prokaryotes have no nucleus. Their DNA sits in an area of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid.

stem: Prokaryotic cells have mitochondria.
explanation: False. Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles, including mitochondria.

stem: Some bacteria move using a long, whip-like tail called a
explanation: A flagellum spins or whips to move the cell. Cilia are short and hair-like.

stem: Which structure is found in eukaryotic cells but NOT in prokaryotic cells?
explanation: The Golgi apparatus is a membrane-bound organelle, so only eukaryotes have it. Both cell types have ribosomes, a membrane, and DNA.

stem: How is DNA usually arranged in a prokaryotic cell?
option_a: Many straight chromosomes inside a nucleus
option_b: A single circular chromosome in the cytoplasm
explanation: Prokaryotes usually have one loop-shaped (circular) chromosome in the nucleoid. Eukaryotes have straight (linear) chromosomes in a nucleus.

stem: Which structures are found in BOTH prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells? Choose all that apply.
explanation: All cells have ribosomes, a cell membrane, DNA, and cytoplasm. Only eukaryotes have a nucleus and mitochondria.

stem: An organism is made of trillions of cells, and each cell has a nucleus. The organism is
explanation: Cells with a nucleus are eukaryotic. All many-celled organisms are eukaryotes.

stem: Yeast is a single-celled fungus with a nucleus. How should it be classified?
explanation: Yeast has a nucleus, so it is eukaryotic, even though it is only one cell.

stem: Which statement about prokaryotes is true?
explanation: All prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) are unicellular. Plants and animals are eukaryotes.

stem: Most bacteria have a cell wall outside their cell membrane.
explanation: True. Most bacteria have a cell wall that protects them and keeps their shape.

stem: Prokaryotes have no mitochondria. Where do their energy reactions happen?
option_b: In the cytoplasm and on the cell membrane
explanation: Without membrane-bound organelles, prokaryotes carry out their energy reactions in the cytoplasm and on their cell membrane.

stem: Some antibiotics stop bacterial ribosomes from working but don't harm human cells much. What is the best explanation?
option_c: Bacterial ribosomes are smaller and built differently from eukaryotic ribosomes
explanation: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic ribosomes differ in size and structure, so a drug can block one kind without blocking the other.

stem: How is the inside of a eukaryotic cell different from the inside of a prokaryotic cell?
option_d: It is divided into compartments by membrane-bound organelles
explanation: A eukaryotic cell's organelles split the cytoplasm into compartments, each with its own job. A prokaryote's inside is one open space.

stem: A cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts, and a nucleus. What kind of cell is it?
explanation: The nucleus and chloroplasts make it eukaryotic, and the cell wall plus chloroplasts point to a plant cell. A cell wall alone does not mean prokaryote.

stem: A student claims, "Any cell with a cell wall must be prokaryotic." Which fact best shows the claim is wrong?
option_b: Plant and fungal cells have cell walls and also have a nucleus
option_c: Animal cells have no cell wall
option_d: Cell walls are made of protein
explanation: Plants and fungi are eukaryotes with cell walls, so having a wall doesn't make a cell prokaryotic.

stem: Think of a prokaryotic cell as a studio apartment (one open room) and a eukaryotic cell as a house with many rooms. What do the rooms in the house stand for?
explanation: Each room is like a membrane-bound organelle: a separate space where certain jobs happen. A prokaryote does everything in one open space.

stem: Which observations would show that a cell is prokaryotic? Choose all that apply.
option_b: Its DNA is in a nucleoid region
explanation: No nucleus, a nucleoid, and no membrane-bound organelles mark a prokaryote. Ribosomes and a cell membrane are in every cell, so they don't help.

stem: Scientists think mitochondria were once free-living prokaryotes. Which evidence supports this idea?
option_b: Mitochondria are found in the nucleus
option_d: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and ribosomes, like bacteria
explanation: Mitochondria have circular DNA and bacteria-like ribosomes, and they divide on their own, which suggests they came from ancient prokaryotes.

stem: Why can eukaryotic cells grow so much larger than prokaryotic cells?
option_a: Membrane-bound organelles and a cytoskeleton organize the cell and move materials around inside it
explanation: In a large cell, materials have far to travel. Organelles divide up the work, and the cytoskeleton moves things where they need to go.

stem: Cell X is 2 micrometers across with no nucleus. Cell Y is 40 micrometers across with a nucleus. Which conclusion is best?
option_a: X is eukaryotic and Y is prokaryotic
option_b: X is prokaryotic and Y is eukaryotic, which fits prokaryotes being smaller
explanation: No nucleus means prokaryotic, and a nucleus means eukaryotic. The sizes fit the usual pattern too.

stem: Which organelle makes most of a cell's usable energy (ATP)?
explanation: Mitochondria release energy from food during cellular respiration and store it as ATP.

stem: Ribosomes are where proteins are made.
explanation: True. Ribosomes read instructions from DNA (carried by RNA) and link amino acids into proteins.

stem: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
explanation: Chloroplasts capture sunlight for photosynthesis. Animal cells don't have them.

stem: What does the large central vacuole do in a plant cell?
option_a: Stores water and helps keep the plant firm
explanation: The central vacuole stores water. When it is full, it pushes against the cell wall and keeps the plant upright.

stem: Which organelle packages proteins into vesicles and ships them to where they are needed?
explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins, a lot like a post office.

stem: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is covered with ribosomes.
explanation: False. Rough ER has ribosomes on its surface; smooth ER does not. Smooth ER makes lipids.

stem: Lysosomes contain
explanation: Lysosomes are full of enzymes that break down food particles, worn-out cell parts, and invaders.

stem: Which path does a protein take when a cell makes it to send outside the cell?
option_d: Ribosome on rough ER → ER → Golgi apparatus → vesicle → cell membrane
explanation: The protein is built by a ribosome on the rough ER, moves through the ER, is packaged by the Golgi, and leaves in a vesicle that joins the cell membrane.

stem: In a model that compares a cell to a factory, the Golgi apparatus is best compared to the
explanation: The Golgi packages and labels proteins and ships them out, just like a factory's shipping department.

stem: In a model that compares a cell to a city, which organelle would be the power plant?
explanation: Mitochondria supply the cell's energy (ATP), just as a power plant supplies a city's electricity.

stem: Which structures are found in animal cells? Choose all that apply.
explanation: Animal cells have a nucleus, mitochondria, and lysosomes. Cell walls and chloroplasts are found in plant cells.

stem: A muscle cell uses a lot of energy. Which organelle would you expect it to have many of?
explanation: More energy needs mean more mitochondria to make ATP.

stem: White blood cells swallow and destroy bacteria. Which organelle would they have many of?
explanation: Lysosomes hold the digestive enzymes that break down the bacteria the white blood cell takes in.

stem: Plant cells have both chloroplasts and mitochondria.
explanation: True. Chloroplasts make sugar from sunlight, and mitochondria release energy from that sugar. Plants need both.

stem: Cells in the pancreas make large amounts of protein enzymes. Which organelles would be especially plentiful in these cells?
explanation: Proteins are built by ribosomes, many of them on the rough ER, so protein-making cells have lots of both.

stem: What would most likely happen if a cell's membrane were badly damaged?
option_a: The cell would make more proteins
option_b: The cell could no longer control what enters and leaves
option_c: The cell would grow a cell wall
explanation: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out. Without it, the cell can't keep its insides separate from its surroundings.

stem: Messages from the nucleus, like RNA, leave the nucleus through
option_c: nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope
explanation: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane with pores that let RNA and other molecules move in and out.

stem: A student's model of an ANIMAL cell includes a cell wall and a large central vacuole. What should the student change?
option_d: Remove the cell wall and the large central vacuole
explanation: Animal cells have no cell wall and only small vacuoles, if any. Those features belong in a plant cell model.

stem: A poison stops a cell's mitochondria from working. What would happen to the cell first?
option_a: It would run low on ATP and couldn't do work that needs energy
option_c: It would grow a cell wall
explanation: Mitochondria make most of a cell's ATP. Without them, energy-using jobs like moving materials and building molecules slow or stop.

stem: Cells in a carrot's root are underground. Which organelle do they lack that cells in a leaf have?
explanation: Root cells get no sunlight, so they don't have chloroplasts. They still have mitochondria to release energy.

stem: A student is building a 3-D model of a PLANT cell. Which parts must be included? Choose all that apply.
explanation: A plant cell model needs a cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole, and a nucleus. Plant cells don't have a flagellum.

stem: A houseplant wilts after a week without water. Which organelle best explains this?
option_b: The mitochondria made too much ATP
option_c: The central vacuoles lost water, so they no longer push against the cell walls
explanation: Full central vacuoles press against the cell walls and keep the plant firm. When they lose water, the plant droops.

stem: A student models an animal cell with a sealed plastic bag filled with gelatin and small objects. What does the gelatin represent?
explanation: The jelly-like gelatin stands for the cytoplasm that fills the cell and holds the organelles. The bag stands for the cell membrane.

stem: A drug breaks down a cell's cytoskeleton. What would most likely happen?
option_a: The cell would lose its shape and have trouble moving its organelles
option_b: The cell would make more ATP
explanation: The cytoskeleton is the cell's framework and its tracks for moving things. Without it, the cell can't hold its shape or move materials well.

stem: In diffusion, particles move from
option_c: inside the nucleus to the cell wall
explanation: Particles naturally spread out from where they are crowded (high concentration) to where they are less crowded (low concentration).

stem: Passive transport requires the cell to use energy (ATP).
explanation: False. Passive transport needs no energy, because substances move down their concentration gradient from high to low.

stem: What does it mean that the cell membrane is selectively permeable?
option_c: It lets some substances through but not others
explanation: Selectively permeable means the membrane chooses: small or needed substances can pass, and others are kept out.

stem: A hypotonic solution has
option_b: a higher solute concentration than the cell
option_c: the same solute concentration as the cell
option_d: a lower solute concentration than the cell
explanation: "Hypo-" means under. A hypotonic solution has less solute (and more water) than the cell, so water moves into the cell.

stem: A cell placed in an isotonic solution will
explanation: In an isotonic solution, the concentrations inside and outside match, so water moves in and out equally.

stem: In an isotonic solution, water still moves in and out of the cell, but there is no net change.
explanation: True. Water molecules keep crossing the membrane both ways at the same rate, so the cell's size doesn't change.

stem: Endocytosis is when a cell
option_b: takes in large particles by wrapping its membrane around them
explanation: In endocytosis, the membrane folds around a large particle and pinches off into a vesicle inside the cell.

stem: A red blood cell is placed in pure (distilled) water. What will happen?
option_c: It will swell and may burst
explanation: Pure water is hypotonic to the cell, so water moves into the cell by osmosis until it swells and may burst.

stem: A plant cell is placed in very salty water. What will happen?
option_a: Water will move into the cell and it will burst
option_d: Water will leave the cell, and the membrane will pull away from the cell wall
explanation: Salty water is hypertonic to the cell, so water leaves by osmosis. The cell wall keeps its shape, but the membrane shrinks inside it.

stem: The sodium-potassium pump moves ions from low concentration to high concentration. What type of transport is this?
explanation: Moving something against its gradient (low to high) takes energy, so it is active transport.

stem: Someone sprays perfume in one corner of a room, and soon it can be smelled across the room. What process is this?
explanation: Perfume molecules spread from where they are concentrated to where they are not. That is diffusion.

stem: Glucose moves into a cell through a carrier protein, from high to low concentration, without using ATP. What type of transport is this?
explanation: It uses a protein but no energy and moves down the gradient, so it is facilitated diffusion.

stem: Which of these require the cell to use energy (ATP)? Choose all that apply.
explanation: Pumps and moving vesicles in or out take energy. Osmosis and simple diffusion are passive.

stem: Small molecules like oxygen and carbon dioxide can diffuse directly through the phospholipid bilayer.
explanation: True. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small and nonpolar, so they slip right between the phospholipids.

stem: Exocytosis is when
option_d: a vesicle joins the cell membrane and releases its contents outside the cell
explanation: In exocytosis, a vesicle fuses with the cell membrane and empties its contents outside, like hormones leaving a gland cell.

stem: Pouring salt on a slug can harm it. Why?
option_a: The salt makes the outside hypertonic, so water leaves the slug's cells by osmosis
option_b: Salt gives the slug too much energy
option_c: Salt enters the cells by active transport
option_d: The salt makes the slug's cells swell
explanation: The salt draws water out of the slug's cells, which dry out.

stem: Which change would make diffusion happen FASTER?
option_c: Making the concentration the same everywhere
explanation: At higher temperatures, particles move faster, so they spread out more quickly.

stem: In the egg lab, an egg with its shell dissolved shrinks in corn syrup and swells in water. Compared with the inside of the egg, corn syrup is
explanation: Water left the egg in corn syrup, so the syrup has more solute than the egg. That makes it hypertonic.

stem: Hospitals give IV fluids that are isotonic to blood instead of pure water. Why?
option_b: Blood cells need extra salt to grow
option_d: Pure water would rush into blood cells by osmosis and could burst them
explanation: Pure water is hypotonic to blood cells. Isotonic fluid keeps water moving in and out evenly, so the cells stay healthy.

stem: A cell contains 5% glucose and sits in a 2% glucose solution. The membrane does not let glucose through. What will happen?
option_a: Water will move into the cell
option_b: Water will move out of the cell
option_c: Glucose will move out of the cell
explanation: Glucose can't move, so water does. The cell has more solute, so water moves in by osmosis toward the higher solute concentration.

stem: A cell moves a molecule from LOW concentration to HIGH concentration. Which must be true? Choose all that apply.
explanation: Moving against the gradient is active transport, which uses protein pumps and energy. Osmosis and diffusion only go from high to low.

stem: Potato pieces changed mass in salt solutions: 0% salt +2.0 g, 1% +0.8 g, 2% 0.0 g, 3% −1.1 g. At about what salt concentration is the solution isotonic to the potato cells?
explanation: At 2% the mass didn't change, so water moved in and out equally. That solution is isotonic to the potato cells.

stem: Why can't a large protein simply diffuse through the cell membrane?
option_b: It is too large to pass through the phospholipid bilayer, so the cell must use vesicles
explanation: Big molecules can't fit between the phospholipids. Cells move them with vesicles (endocytosis and exocytosis).

stem: Freshwater protists like paramecia have contractile vacuoles that pump out water. Why do they need them?
option_a: They make water in their mitochondria
option_b: Their surroundings are hypertonic, so they keep losing water
option_c: Their surroundings are hypotonic, so water keeps flowing in by osmosis
explanation: Freshwater has less solute than the cell, so water keeps entering. The contractile vacuole pumps out the extra so the cell doesn't burst.
